title: The bigger joy (290–295)
hook: if by leaving a small pleasure one finds a great one, the wise leave the small

segments.voice: Yesterday, vana: forest and desire both, so cut the whole wanting, not one tree. Your line was cut the forest. Today, chapter twenty-one begins.

There's a famous experiment with children and marshmallows: one now, or two if you can wait. The same trade turns up at the dinner table, when the phone buzzes while the person across from you is mid-story. Or the extra hour in bed, when the quiet morning walk was the plan. The small pleasure isn't evil. It just sits right in front of the bigger one, blocking the view. A chapter the translator simply called miscellaneous opens with exactly this trade.
screen: `ONE MARSHMALLOW NOW, OR TWO?` → `THE SMALL PLEASURE BLOCKS THE VIEW.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED MISCELLANEOUS.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-one gathers verses that didn't fit elsewhere, and it starts with a plain one. Verse two hundred ninety, in Max Müller's English: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." Notice the verse doesn't say pleasure is bad. The Pali word is sukha: happiness, ease, sweetness. The verse wants more of it, not less. It's a trade, and the wise person makes the good one. The next verse shows a bad trade: the one who seeks happiness for himself by causing pain to others gets tangled up in hatred and never gets free. Then the verses turn to attention. People neglect what ought to be done and do what ought not, the text says, and their desires keep growing; but those who keep watch over the body, moment by moment, don't drift that way. Then comes a startling pair, verses two hundred ninety-four and two hundred ninety-five. They say the true brahmana goes free, even after killing mother and father and two kings. Read on its own, it's shocking. The old commentary explains it as a riddle. The mother is craving, the father is pride, the kings are two wrong views, and the kingdom is the senses and everything that rides on them. Kill those, and you walk free. It's yesterday's forest, told as a riddle. The bigger joy, in the end, is the freedom on the far side of all the small trades.
screen: `SUKHA — HAPPINESS, EASE, SWEETNESS.` · `A BAD TRADE: JOY BUILT ON PAIN.` · `KEEP WATCH OVER THE BODY.` · `THE RIDDLE OF MOTHER, FATHER, KINGS.` · then, large: `THE BIGGER JOY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small pleasure you reach for most days, a second coffee, one more episode, a few more minutes in bed, and ask what bigger joy it sometimes stands in front of: a conversation, a rested morning, a clear head. You don't have to give anything up; just see the two side by side, the small and the great. Then let both go, and rest in the breath, which asks nothing of you.
Sukha. Happiness, ease: leave a small sukha when it hides a great one; the verse wants more happiness, not less.
Your line: look to the great. Small joy and great joy are both sukha. Day two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use verse 290 to explain renunciation not as loss but as trading a lesser happiness for a greater one; the riddle verses 294–295 are usually taught with the commentary's symbolic reading.

original.note: Pali sukha: happiness, ease; verse 290 speaks of small sukha and great sukha.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism asks you to give up pleasure.
what it means: verse 290 asks you to trade a small happiness for a greater one.
what a scholar hears: 'mattasukha' (a measured, small happiness) against 'vipulam sukham' (vast happiness): the verse weighs one against the other.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook no longer tells the listener what they feel; 'one of the clearest in the book' and 'the strangest pair of verses in the whole book' cut (superlatives); verse 292 paraphrase corrected to the text's 'desires keep growing' (was 'troubles grow'); practice examples changed so the snack image doesn't repeat day 211; trapdoor's unverified claim that the commentary pairs 290 with 294–295 removed.
Müller's verse 290 verified exact against Gutenberg #2017.

The commentary's reading of 294–295: mother = craving, father = conceit/pride, two kings = eternalism and annihilationism views, kingdom = the sense bases with their objects; 295 adds the tiger (the hindrance of doubt). Confirm.
